name: Bay
lede: Bay is a moderate reddish brown recorded across six color systems since 1821.

sections.title: Six systems, one brown
sections.body:
Bay is the rare case among nature names with a paper trail. Our library lists it in Werner's 1821 nomenclature, Ridgway's 1886 and 1912 color standards, the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, and the RAL system of 1927, with Ridgway's 1912 plate II, hue 7, as the best-documented swatch [1]. Werner's chart, by Syme's account, ties no. 103 of the Browns to three everyday things: the neck and breast of the red grouse, chestnuts, and Egyptian jasper [3].

Ridgway's own 1912 swatch runs a little darker than ours (#6F574C), and RAL's is darker still (#633A34); our library lists Chestnut Brown and Signal Brown as near-duplicates, 2.0 and 2.4 ΔE away [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[tortoise]], [[auburn]], [[coffee]] and [[mahogany-red]], at 2.7, 4, 4 and 4.3 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to Bay in 1,836 of 23,781 paintings (7.72 percent), as photographed, the within-painting reading at 904, making it more common than 89 percent of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 55 of 945 paintings, at 1.6 times the overall rate, and it is over-represented in paintings from Tibet, at 5.5 times the expected rate [2].

George Catlin, who painted Native American subjects, used it most: 9 of his 50 works here, 4.4 times his home museums' baseline [2]. It most often plays an accent inside a painting, and keeps company with [[brownish]] and [[chocolate-red]] more than chance [2]. These are screen approximations of aged, varnished canvases, not pigment identifications [2].
